meta.title: Linear vs. Exponential: AGI Has Arrived But Oil, Bonds and the Fed Oh My
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · why rates/oil are noise now, AGI's arrival via Astra, the GPU-depreciation bear case being wrong, the case for Ethereum, Robinhood's tokenization convergence, and building your own AI trading system

snapshot: Core CPI and PPI both beat, Fed-hike odds and oil rose, and the S&P was still up over two days — Visser's proof that **oil/bonds/Fed** stopped driving markets in 2008 and AI capex now does.
Jensen Huang says **AGI has arrived** with Astra (trained on 100k GPUs; the next model is 4x the size); agents reportedly cracked the Navier-Stokes problem using 10,000 agents over 88 hours.
H100 rental prices are roughly unchanged in three years and **up 22% this month alone** — the opposite of what depreciation bears (Burry, Chanos) assumed, per Gavin Baker's thesis.
Ethereum broke out to its **highest level since January** and Visser argues it should keep outperforming Bitcoin in this cycle because of network effects plus the agentic/AI-agent use case.
Robinhood Chain, live only two months, is already generating **$6M/day in fees** and rerating the on-chain market; Bernstein sees 31% upside for Robinhood shares.
A wave of AI-enabled hacks (UK power plant, Boston Scientific, Anthropic's Opus flagging Iran targeting US Navy ships) feeds Visser's separate long-term bull case for crypto as a **trust layer**.
Visser built and back-tested his own AI-agent trading system this week (Astra + Robinhood/Moomoo/Interactive Brokers) and is sharing the workflow so subscribers' kids can build their own.
Personal note: the episode opens and closes with a 9/11 tribute to a close friend Visser lost 25 years ago.

themes.title: Oil, bonds and the Fed stopped being the story in 2008 — AI capex is
themes.lead: The market shrugged off hot inflation data and rising rate-hike odds this week, and Visser says that's the whole point: you're either trading the old linear economy or the new AI-capex one.
bullets: This week: core CPI and PPI both came in **higher than expected**, Fed rate-hike odds jumped (Jackson Hole odds cited at up to 90%), oil rose, and the war news worsened — yet the S&P was up slightly over the two days. Old linear inputs didn't move the tape.

Visser dates the regime change to **2008**: the iPhone's release the year before plus a sharp rise in government transfer payments/debt ended the old housing-and-autos economy that oil/bonds/rates actually drove.

Credit confirms it: **HYG relative to IEF** (his real-time credit-spread proxy) isn't falling even as bonds sell off — contrast with 2022, when credit sold off *alongside* equities as the Fed hiked aggressively.

Bessent is openly fighting the bond market (upsizing buybacks, coordinating with Japan's finance minister, daring Fed's Warsh) — a deliberate signal the administration doesn't want, or need, higher rates to matter.
Bitcoin Policy angle: Bessent's own framing — **"there is no day after tomorrow if China wins"** the AI race — is Visser's justification for not fighting either the AI trade or the crypto trade.

quote.text: AGI has arrived. That should be the big news story of the week. It shouldn't be whether bond yields were up 10 basis points, whether oil was up $10.

themes.watch: This is Visser's own framing of what "matters" — he is explicitly arguing against mainstream macro commentary (Goldman/Morgan Stanley rate forecasts), not reporting a consensus view.

themes.title: Jensen Huang: AGI has arrived with Astra — and agents reportedly solved Navier-Stokes
themes.lead: Between OpenAI's Astra release and a reported multi-agent solve of a 200-year-old physics problem, Visser treats this as the week AI crossed from "impressive" to "agentic."
bullets: Astra was trained on **100,000 GPUs**; the next model is roughly 4x that size, with Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips behind it.
Research agents are now reportedly generating the equivalent of **3.1 workdays of output per human workday**.

10,000 AI agents working in parallel for **88 hours** reportedly cracked the Navier-Stokes problem — a longstanding fluid-dynamics challenge with claimed knock-on implications for turbines, aircraft, cooling systems, batteries and reactor design.

OpenAI's Greg Brockman (in a 24-minute interview) describes Astra as merging chat, agents, desktop and Codex into one system — Visser's read: this is the point knowledge workers (he names accountants specifically) need to start paying attention.

Visser's framework: GDP has always been people + capital + productivity; AI adds *digital labor* that doesn't take breaks, so the constraint shifts to **compute and energy**, not headcount — and he argues GDP itself (a 1930s industrial-output metric) is the wrong tool to measure this productivity gain.

The corollary he draws for equities: as AI shortens **corporate duration** (how long a business can keep growing before disruption), terminal value and multiples compress — which is why he's fine with Nvidia and Micron's multiples compressing even while the businesses do well.

quote.text: We're really trying to empower the individual to make it so that you can have superpowers, you can accomplish more.

themes.watch: The Navier-Stokes "solve" and the 3.1x research-agent productivity figure are as reported in coverage Visser read this week, not independently verified by him.

themes.title: The GPU-depreciation bear case (Burry, Chanos) looks wrong — rental prices are rising
themes.lead: Visser stacks up evidence that H100 rental prices have not fallen the way depreciation-schedule bears assumed, and argues that flips the hyperscaler credit story.
bullets: H100 rental prices are **almost unchanged from three years ago**, when the normal aging curve would have implied a 40-50% decline by now.
Rental prices are **up 22% this month alone**, per Gavin Baker's thesis (which Visser flagged a month ago) that the market wrongly assumed GPU rental rates would steadily fall.

Visser's tomato analogy: chips bought at "$2" are now rented out at "$6" of compute value — hyperscalers get to *reprice* existing fleets as old contracts roll off, rather than eating a falling asset value.

Baker's point, per Visser: this could remove **hundreds of billions of dollars** of expected hyperscaler credit/financing needs if cash flow from repricing existing compute is this much higher than modeled.
This directly rebuts the Michael Burry/Jim Chanos accounting argument that H100 depreciation schedules were too generous because chip value would collapse within a few years.
Microsoft's reiterated capacity shortage this week is cited as corroborating evidence that demand — not oversupply — is still the binding constraint.
themes.watch: This is Visser relaying Gavin Baker's thesis and his own read of rental-price data, not an independent audit of hyperscaler books; Paul Tudor Jones's more skeptical note on AI this week is mentioned but not engaged with in detail.

themes.title: How Visser values Ethereum: network effects, trust, and an Amazon-in-1997 analogy
themes.lead: Ethereum just broke out to its highest level since January, and Visser lays out five to six reasons he thinks it deserves to keep outperforming Bitcoin in this cycle.
bullets: **Network-effect + agentic case:** Ethereum broke out to its highest level since January during "a huge week for Ethereum over Bitcoin"; Visser argues Ethereum should outperform Bitcoin in a real bull market because the ecosystem/network effect is the critical value driver, and the agentic AI use case (especially post-Astra) strengthens that.

**Institutional rails are choosing it live:** Robinhood Chain (built on Arbitrum, an Ethereum layer-2) already does $6M/day in fees after two months; European banks are separately planning to launch a euro stablecoin **on Ethereum** this same week — concrete money choosing Ethereum's rails, not just price speculation.

**The original 2014-15 thesis is aging well:** William Mougayar's decade-old TED talk on Ethereum/blockchain gets an 8/10 on direction and 5/10 on specifics from Visser — good for something made under years of regulatory uncertainty. Mougayar missed stablecoins and, crucially, missed AI agents — which Visser argues may be exactly what finally makes Mougayar's original disintermediation thesis work, since agents (unlike humans) actually need trustless rails.

**No earnings model fits yet — that's normal, not disqualifying:** per Mougayar's second talk ("Ethereum's Endgame"), crypto valuation is going through the same phase the early internet did — eyeballs, then revenue, then (25 years later) SaaS metrics. Ethereum's value drivers today are network effects, ecosystem value, productive assets, flow of money, and programmability, not a P/E.

**The Amazon-in-1997 analogy:** Amazon ran with no P/E (or none below 100) from 1997 until 2017-18, and is up roughly 27,000% from its 1997 lows; Ethereum is up about 3,000% from its own lows. Visser's read: the market will eventually give up trying to value Ethereum on old terms the same way it did with Amazon, and that capitulation point is still ahead, not behind.

**Trust as the asset:** Mougayar's forthcoming book ("Trust Shift") argues AI turns trust itself into an economic asset; Visser's extension is that any real-world asset that needs verifiable trust will eventually need to sit on Ethereum, and the current wave of AI-enabled hacking (see Other Notable News) is part of why he holds this even more strongly.

quote.text: I really do believe we're going to see a similar number at a similar time where someone who's in TradFi is finally going to give up and say, 'I don't understand how to value this thing.'

themes.watch: Visser flags his own history here as a caution, not an endorsement of timing it perfectly: he was macro/oil-focused and dismissed Amazon as un-investable at the time, by his own account.

themes.title: Robinhood is becoming the AI-crypto-TradFi convergence play, Visser argues
themes.lead: Visser calls Robinhood the epicenter of an AI/crypto/macro nexus and lays out the same week's tokenization news as evidence the shift is already underway industry-wide.
bullets: Robinhood Chain has been live only two months and already generates **$6M/day in fees**, already rerating the on-chain market; Bernstein sees 31% upside for Robinhood shares as its fees overtake Solana's.
Arbitrum, the app layer riding on Robinhood Chain, surged **7.87%** on the news — and Visser notes the Wall Street Journal had zero coverage of it, framing TradFi media as behind the story.

Robinhood struck a deal with Crypto.com this week and presented at the Goldman Sachs technology conference with five stated priorities: agentic trading going mainstream, Robinhood Chain as global financial infrastructure, wanting the *entire* financial relationship (trading, crypto, retirement, banking), and prediction markets as a "gateway product."
Visser's framing: Robinhood is evolving from a brokerage app into an **AI-native tokenized financial platform** — he explicitly compares the strategy to Apple's ecosystem playbook.

The same week's broader confirmation: Nasdaq invested $100M in Kraken eyeing 2027 tokenized-stock trading; US Bank is testing stablecoins; Visa's stablecoin card business is "exploding"; Coinbase's Brian Armstrong and Patrick Witt both said the Clarity Act is ready for a yes vote.
Visser's own probability read is more conservative than the public optimism: he puts the odds of the Clarity Act passing this year at **under 20%**, even though he thinks it can still get a yes vote.

themes.watch: The Clarity Act probability and the Apple-strategy comparison are Visser's own estimates, not something Robinhood itself has stated.

themes.title: Visser built his own AI-agent trading system this week — and is sharing the workflow
themes.lead: Triggered by Astra's release, Visser built and back-tested an AI-agent trading desk and is walking subscribers through replicating it on Robinhood, Moomoo or Interactive Brokers.
bullets: He ran six AI agents (including ones he calls "Probe" and "Prism") against a real account, seeding it with **$500** and reporting **$5,100** by the next morning — presented as a demo, not a claim people should expect to replicate.

His filtering logic mirrors how multi-strat hedge funds vet ideas: thousands of daily ideas, **99% rejected** at the first pass, then another 90% of the survivors rejected — the design goal is rejection, not idea volume.

His own technical model layers **rate-of-change, ATR (average true range) and a structural-trend/reset cycle** on a 100-stock AI-buildout universe (he notes 80%+ of those names are above a rising 200-day moving average).

He explicitly does not expect repeats of this year's biggest winners (e.g., no expectation Micron repeats its 5x/12-bagger move) and expects multiple compression to make old buy-and-hold approaches harder, with most trading days flat or down and just ~5% of days driving the year's return.

Practical path he lays out: build on GitHub, test small dollar amounts ($50-100) across multiple uncorrelated strategies to create a mini multi-strat, paper-trade first via Robinhood/Moomoo/Interactive Brokers agentic tools, then scale.
themes.watch: The $500-to-$5,100 result and the back-test performance are self-reported from Visser's own build this week, not independently audited.

takeaways.title: Stop reading rate/oil headlines as the market driver — track AI capex, the HYG/IEF credit-spread proxy, and profit-margin revisions instead.
Watch Greg Brockman's 24-minute Astra interview before assuming you understand what "merging chat, agents and desktop" actually changes for your workflow.
Re-evaluate Ethereum on network-effects/ecosystem terms, not a P/E lens — Visser frames the current no-earnings phase as Amazon's 1997-2013 run, not a red flag.
If you're on Robinhood, Moomoo or Interactive Brokers, paper-trade one small AI-agent strategy before committing real size, then layer in more uncorrelated ones.
If your job is knowledge work you're not attached to, start building your own AI/GitHub automation now — Visser cites Sundar Pichai's warning that non-adopters spend 2027 catching up.
Track the Clarity Act as a near-term catalyst, but temper expectations — Visser puts 2026 passage odds under 20% despite public optimism from Coinbase and Robinhood executives.
